findings.risk: A dependency declared with an HTTP or FTP URL in package.json is fetched without TLS encryption, allowing a man-in-the-middle attacker to replace the package with malicious code that runs during npm install (CWE-300, CWE-319, CWE-494, CWE-829).
findings.solution: Replace HTTP/FTP dependency URLs with HTTPS equivalents, or better, publish the package to npm and reference it by name and version.
findings.benefit: Prevents man-in-the-middle attacks replacing npm dependencies with malicious code.

findings.risk: Logging sensitive values (passwords, tokens, secrets) writes them in cleartext to log files, log aggregation systems, and stdout — logs are often retained long-term, accessible to monitoring tools, and may be stored insecurely in cloud logging services (CWE-312, CWE-315, CWE-359).
findings.solution: Never log raw sensitive values. Mask or redact sensitive fields before logging: log the presence ("token present: true"), not the value. Use structured logging with field-level redaction.
findings.benefit: Prevents sensitive data exposure via application log files and log aggregation systems.

findings.solution: Remove useless escapes or use raw string literals (template literals) to avoid inadvertent escape interpretation. Verify each escape sequence is intentional.
findings.benefit: Ensures regex patterns match exactly the intended characters without silent escaping bugs.

findings.benefit: Prevents XSS via alternative executable URL schemes bypassing incomplete scheme checks.

findings.risk: An async database query inside a loop triggers one query per iteration — N+1 queries for N records. This causes exponential load on the database, response time degradation, and potential denial of service under traffic (CWE-770).
findings.solution: Use bulk fetching: collect all IDs first, then fetch with a single IN query or findAll({ where: { id: ids } }). For ORMs: use eager loading (include) to fetch related data in a single query.
findings.benefit: Reduces database load from O(N) queries to O(1), drastically improving response time and scalability.

findings.risk: A <button> without a type attribute defaults to type="submit" in most browsers. Inside a form, this causes the button to submit the form when clicked, even if its purpose is something else (e.g. open a modal, toggle a menu). This leads to accidental form submissions that are hard to debug.
findings.solution: Always specify the type attribute. Use type="button" for buttons that trigger actions, type="submit" for form submission buttons, and type="reset" for form reset buttons.
findings.benefit: Explicit, predictable button behavior — no accidental form submissions, clear intent for every button in the codebase.

findings.risk: Links with target="_blank" without rel="noopener noreferrer" allow the newly opened page to access the opener window via window.opener. This creates a security vulnerability (reverse tabnapping) and a privacy leak (the referrer URL is sent to the target site).
findings.solution: Always add rel="noopener noreferrer" to every link with target="_blank". Modern browsers apply noopener automatically, but the explicit declaration ensures compatibility and prevents referrer leaks.
findings.benefit: Prevents reverse tabnapping attacks and referrer leaks — third-party sites opened in new tabs cannot manipulate the original page.

findings.rule: JSX label without associated control (missing htmlFor)
findings.risk: A JSX <label> without a htmlFor prop (or an associated control as a child) is not programmatically linked to its form control. Screen readers cannot associate the label with the input, making the form inaccessible.
findings.solution: Add a htmlFor prop matching the id of the associated input. Alternatively, nest the input directly inside the label (implicit association).
findings.benefit: Compliance with WCAG 1.3.1 and 4.1.2 — clicking the label focuses the associated input, and screen readers announce the label when the input is focused.

findings.risk: A public class without a docstring forces developers to read the implementation to understand its purpose, interface, and usage. This slows down onboarding and code reviews.
